drills.q: What is BOLA, why has it remained #1 on OWASP's API Top 10 since 2019, and how would you find it in a codebase you just joined?
drills.a: BOLA is a missing object-level authorization check -- the caller is authenticated but ownership of the specific requested object is never verified. Remains #1 since it requires no sophisticated technique (increment an ID) and is trivially introduced by forgetting one check. To find it: for every endpoint accepting an object ID, write an automated test asserting a SECOND, non-owning identity is rejected -- manual testing with one account per tester tends to miss this.

drills.q: Your API gateway validates every token before requests reach your service. Doesn't that cover BOLA?
drills.a: No -- the gateway validates token structural validity and rate limits (authentication and coarse authorization), but has no business-logic knowledge of which specific object a given subject legitimately owns. That check can only be implemented at the service layer with access to the actual data model.

drills.q: Explain mass assignment and why it's dangerous even with zero SQL injection vulnerabilities.
drills.a: An endpoint binds the entire client-supplied request body onto an internal model with no allowlist, so a client can set fields never meant to be client-writable (is_admin, role) simply by including them in the JSON -- entirely independent of query parameterization. It's an authorization gap at the property level, not an injection vulnerability. Fix: framework serializer/schema layer enforcing an explicit writable-field allowlist.

drills.q: What's the difference between BOLA (API1) and Broken Function Level Authorization (API5)?
drills.a: BOLA is about which OBJECT a caller can access (allowed to call the endpoint generally, shouldn't access this specific instance). API5 is about whether the caller can invoke the FUNCTION/endpoint at all -- e.g. an admin route callable by any user because the restriction only existed in the UI, never server-side. The two can compound on the same endpoint.

drills.q: Design rate limiting for a public API and explain why it doesn't fully address API6 (unrestricted business flows).
drills.a: Standard per-token/per-IP rate limiting defends against single-source automation, but a sophisticated attacker distributes requests across many accounts/IPs to stay under any single threshold, each request individually looking legitimate. Address with controls tied to a durable identity signal: verified-account caps, behavioral/device fingerprinting, CAPTCHA/proof-of-work at high-automation-risk points.

drills.q: A colleague says the API gateway's auth/rate-limiting layer means services don't need their own authorization logic. Evaluate.
drills.a: The gateway enforces token validity and rate budgets but has no visibility into your data model -- it can't know order 12345 belongs to user A, not B, since that's application-specific business data. Object/function-level authorization must live in the service with access to ownership data; the gateway is a necessary complement, not a substitute.

drills.q: Why is 'the client just won't display the extra fields' not a security control for excessive data exposure?
drills.a: If an endpoint serializes and returns the entire internal object, that data is fully present in the raw HTTP response and trivially visible via dev tools, a proxy, or curl, regardless of what the intended client renders. Client-side filtering is a UX layer with zero enforcement power; the server must withhold fields via an explicit read-side allowlist.

drills.q: What's the GraphQL-specific flavor of unrestricted resource consumption, and how do you defend against it?
drills.a: A single deeply-nested recursive query can cause combinatorial database fan-out while looking like one request to a standard rate limiter. Defense requires GraphQL-specific query complexity/depth analysis, assigning a cost per field/relation and rejecting queries exceeding a configured maximum, in addition to standard rate limiting.

drills.q: A pentest finds API v1's known vulnerability still exploitable 18 months after v1 was 'deprecated' in docs and v2 shipped a fix. What happened, and what's the fix going forward?
drills.a: This is API9's failure mode: 'deprecated in documentation' and 'actually decommissioned' are different things. Some consumers never migrated, the route was never removed, and v1 quietly kept serving live traffic with the known vulnerability. Fix: enforce a decommission date with monitoring confirming zero remaining traffic before removal, not just an announcement.

drills.q: Design authorization for a multi-tenant SaaS API where users should only see their own tenant's data, layered with per-user ownership within that tenant.
drills.a: Two layers: first, every query scoped to the caller's tenant ID derived from the VERIFIED TOKEN, never a client-supplied parameter, ideally enforced via database-layer row-level security as a structural backstop (not just an application-layer WHERE clause that one forgotten query path could skip). Second, within the correctly tenant-scoped result set, the standard per-object ownership check still applies exactly as in the single-tenant case.

drills.q: A junior engineer says 'our API only accepts requests from our official mobile app, so most of the OWASP API Top 10 doesn't apply.' Respond.
drills.a: A server has no reliable way to verify a request originated from the official app rather than a reverse-engineered client or replayed traffic captured elsewhere -- any client-side identifier can be extracted or spoofed. Every control in the list applies regardless of assumed client, because the server can only act on what actually arrives. App attestation (App Attest/Play Integrity) helps but attests the CLIENT, not the specific request's authorization, so it's complementary, never a substitute for object/function-level checks.
